title: How to Get Out of Payday Loan Debt
description: How to get out of payday loan debt: stop the rollovers, ask for an extended payment plan, protect your bank account, and find free help.
keywords: how to get out of payday loan debt payday loan rollover extended payment plan stop payday loan debit
takeaways: Payday loans often cost an APR of almost 400%. The rollover is what keeps people stuck.
Ask the lender for an extended payment plan before you roll over again.
Once it is paid off, point that payment into a small emergency fund.
body:
If a payday loan is due and there is not enough in your account to cover it, take a breath. You are not careless, and you are not the only person in this spot. These loans are set up in a way that makes them hard to finish. The whole amount, plus the fee, lands on your next payday, the same day rent, food, and every other bill still need paying. So the loan rolls over, the fee repeats, and the balance stays exactly where it was.

The way out is rarely one big payment. It is a short list of moves, done in the right order, and most of them happen in the next seven days. You ask for a payment plan before the due date. You take back control of your bank account. You protect the money for rent and food first. Then you bring in free help.

## Why these loans are so hard to shake

A payday loan is usually small, often $500 or less, and it is normally due in one single payment on your next payday, two to four weeks after you took it out. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) notes that fees commonly run from $10 to $30 for every $100 borrowed, and that a typical two week loan with a $15 per $100 fee works out to an APR of almost 400 percent. Credit cards, for comparison, usually sit between about 12 and 30 percent APR.

The real problem is the shape of the payment. One large lump sum, taken in full, on the one day your other bills also land. If you cannot pay it, many lenders offer a rollover. You pay the fee again and the due date moves. Your balance does not drop by a single cent. The fee buys you time, and nothing else. That is the trap, and it is why the order of your next few moves matters more than the size of any one payment.

## The escape order: your first 7 days

Do these in this order. The sequence matters because each step protects the next one.

| Order | Move                                                                   | When to do it                                  |
|-------|------------------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| 1     | Ask the lender for an extended payment plan                            | Before the due date, the earlier the better    |
| 2     | Revoke the automatic debit in writing, and tell your bank              | At least 3 business days before the next debit |
| 3     | Set aside rent, food, and utility money where the loan cannot touch it | Today                                          |
| 4     | Call a free debt advice service                                        | This week, before the due date if you can      |

None of this needs money you do not have. Steps 1, 2, and 4 cost nothing but a phone call or a letter.

## Step 1: Ask for an extended payment plan before the due date

This is the single most useful call you can make, and it has to happen before the loan is due. The CFPB's advice is plain: if you are having trouble repaying, contact your lender right away and ask for an extended repayment plan, or ask what other options exist.

An extended payment plan splits what you owe into smaller installments over a longer period, instead of one lump sum. Whether you can get one depends on your state law or the lender's own policy. In a number of states, lenders are required to offer one when a borrower asks. The plan may be free, or it may carry a small extra fee, again depending on state law. Lenders do not always volunteer this option, so ask directly.

On the call, keep it simple. Say you cannot repay in full on the due date and you want an extended payment plan. Then ask three things. How many installments, and on which dates? Is there any extra fee, yes or no? And can you have the agreement in writing before you agree to it? Do not accept a new loan or a rollover as the answer. A plan pays the same debt down. A rollover charges you again to owe it.

If the person on the phone says no plan exists, do not argue. Note the date, time, and name, and move to step 4 below. A credit counselor or your state regulator can tell you what your state actually requires.

## Step 2: Revoke the automatic debit, properly and in writing

When you took the loan, you almost certainly gave the lender permission to take money straight from your bank account. Under US federal law, you can take that permission back. The CFPB is clear: you have the right to stop a company from taking automatic payments from your account, even if you allowed them before. Doing it properly takes three short actions.

### 1. Tell the lender, in writing

Call the lender and say you are revoking their authorization to debit your account. Then follow up in writing and keep a copy. A spoken request is easy to dispute later. A dated letter is not. The CFPB publishes free sample letters for exactly this on its website.

### 2. Tell your bank or credit union

Next, contact your bank and tell them you have revoked the lender's authorization. Give them a copy of your letter to the lender. If the due date is close, also give your bank a stop payment order, a direct instruction not to allow that payment. To stop the next scheduled payment, your bank needs the order at least three business days before the payment date. If you give it by phone, your bank may ask you to confirm in writing within 14 days, so ask what they need and send it the same day.

### 3. Watch the account

Check your account on the day the debit was due and for a few days after. If money comes out after you revoked authorization, contact your bank right away. You have the right to dispute an unauthorized transfer and get the money back, as long as you report it promptly.

Two honest warnings. First, banks often charge a fee for a stop payment order, so ask what it costs. It is still usually far less than a string of overdraft fees. Second, revoking the debit does not cancel the debt. You still owe the money, and the lender can pursue it another way, including in court. What revoking does is put the timing back in your hands, so the loan stops helping itself to money meant for rent. That is why it works best alongside step 1, a real agreed plan.

## Step 3: Protect rent and food money first

While you sort the loan out, decide in advance what the loan does not get to touch. Rent or mortgage, food, basic utilities, and the cost of getting to work come first. A payday loan is unsecured debt. Your home and your job keep you able to pay anything at all, so they get paid before a lender does.

In practice, this means two things. Keep enough in your account for the essentials, or move that money to a separate account if you have one, so a stray debit cannot clear it out. And if keeping the essentials means another bill will be late, call that company too. Landlords, utility companies, and card issuers all have hardship processes, and a short call before a missed payment usually goes better than silence after one. Our guide to [how to avoid bank fees](/blog/avoid-bank-fees/) explains how to stop one failed debit from turning into a pile of bank charges.

## Step 4: Get free help from people who do this daily

You do not have to work this out alone, and you should not have to pay for advice. Free, nonprofit help exists in each country this site covers.

- In the US, nonprofit credit counseling agencies, many of them members of the National Foundation for Credit Counseling (NFCC), offer a first session free or at low cost. A counselor can review your whole budget, talk to lenders with you, and, where it fits, set up a debt management plan that replaces several payments with one.
- In the UK, StepChange Debt Charity gives free debt advice online and by phone, and it deals with payday lenders every day.
- In Australia, the National Debt Helpline (1800 007 007) offers free, confidential financial counselling and step by step guides for common debts, including payday loans.

A counselor also helps you spot the wrong kind of help. Be wary of any company that wants an upfront fee to settle your payday loans, or that tells you to stop paying lenders while it keeps your money. Legitimate nonprofit help does not work that way. If a lender or collector mistreats you, US readers can file a complaint with the CFPB online or at (855) 411-2372.

## What not to do this week

Three moves feel helpful and are not. Do not take a second payday loan to pay the first one. The fees stack, and you now owe two lenders. Do not pay a rollover fee without asking about a payment plan first, since the plan is often free where the rollover is not. And do not ignore the loan and hope. An unpaid balance can go to collections, and dealing with step 1 now, while the loan is current, is easier than dealing with a collector later. If other debts are crowding in too, [debt snowball vs avalanche](/blog/debt-snowball-vs-avalanche/) lays out two ways to order them once this loan is under control.

## A worked example: rollover versus payment plan

Here is an illustration with made up numbers. Say you borrowed $400 with a $60 fee, so $460 is due in two weeks.

With rollovers, you pay $60 on the due date to extend, another $60 two weeks later, and then the full $460 when you finally clear it. Total paid: $580, for $400 of borrowing, and for a month the balance never moved.

With an extended payment plan, the same $460 is split into four installments of $115 across four paydays, with no extra fee in this example. Total paid: $460. That is $120 less than the rollover path, and every payment actually lowers what you owe. Plans and fees vary by state and lender, which is why the written terms in step 1 matter, but the pattern holds almost everywhere: a plan ends the loan, a rollover rents it.

## Once the loan is gone

When the last installment clears, you get a payday back that is actually yours. Before it fills up with ordinary spending, point the amount you were paying toward a small starter emergency fund, even $200 or $300 in a separate account. That cushion is what stands between a broken car and another payday loan next time. [How to build an emergency fund on a small income](/blog/emergency-fund-on-a-small-income/) shows how to build one on a tight budget, and [how to budget on less than $1,000 a month](/blog/budget-on-less-than-1000-a-month/) helps you reshape the month so it keeps growing.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does revoking the debit cancel my loan?

No. You still owe the money. Revoking only stops the lender from taking payments straight out of your account. You then pay another way, ideally through the extended payment plan you agreed in step 1.

### Can I be sent to jail for not paying a payday loan?

Unpaid consumer debt is a civil matter, not a criminal one. A lender can sue you in civil court, which is serious enough, but a collector who threatens arrest is waving a red flag. Report threats like that to the CFPB or your state attorney general.

### What if my lender refuses to offer a payment plan?

Ask what your state requires. Some states make lenders offer one, and a counselor from the NFCC, or free legal aid in your area, can tell you where you stand. You can also complain to the CFPB, which forwards complaints to the company.

### Will stopping the debit hurt my credit score?

It can, indirectly. If the loan stays unpaid, the account may go to collections, and a collection can be reported on your credit file. That is why revoking the debit should come with a plan to pay, not on its own.

### Should I close my bank account to stop the lender?

Treat that as a last resort, and talk to your bank first. Revoking authorization in writing plus a stop payment order usually does the job, without the disruption of closing an account and setting up direct deposits all over again.

### I already missed the due date. Is it too late?

No. The order still works. Call the lender and ask what plan is available now, protect your essential bills, and bring in a free counselor soon. Options narrow as fees and collection activity build, so this week is still much better than next month.

A quick note: this article is general information about dealing with payday loan debt, not personal financial or legal advice. Loan rules differ by state and country, so check your own agreement and local rules, or ask a nonprofit counselor or legal aid service about your situation.
